prompt: `total = 0` ran once, then `total = total + 10; total` ran three times. What does the last run show?
hint: Each run starts from where the last one left `total`.

prompt: What is the number in brackets beside a cell?
hint: It is the kernel's, not the page's.

choices.text: The cell's position on the page
choices.why: Position and count only agree in a notebook run once from the top.

choices.text: How many times this cell has been run
choices.why: It counts every cell the kernel ran, not this one's runs.

choices.text: The kernel's tally when it ran this cell
choices.why: Right. It is the only record of order on the page.

choices.text: The number of lines of output the cell produced
choices.why: Output length is not recorded anywhere beside the cell.

prompt: A notebook shows counts `[1]`, `[2]`, `[9]`, `[10]` down the page. What should you suspect?
hint: Six runs happened somewhere.

choices.text: Cells ran in between, out of page order
choices.why: Right. Counts 3 to 8 went to cells that were rerun or deleted.

choices.text: Nothing: counts only need to increase
choices.why: Increasing is not enough; a gap means runs you cannot see.

choices.text: The kernel crashed after the second cell and was started again
choices.why: A new kernel starts counting at 1 again.

choices.text: The third and fourth cells are Markdown
choices.why: Markdown cells get no count at all.

prompt: IPython keeps every cell's input, in the order it ran, in a list called `___`.
hint: Two letters, capital first.

prompt: Ana's saved notebook has counts `1`, `4`, `3`. Why is the second cell's count higher than the third's?
hint: The count is from the cell's last run.

choices.text: The third cell was added first
choices.why: It was added after the second failed.

choices.text: JupyterLab numbers cells from the bottom
choices.why: It numbers runs, in the order they happen.

choices.text: Counts are random identifiers, like cell ids
choices.why: Ids are random; counts are a tally.

choices.text: It was rerun later
choices.why: Right: run 2 failed, run 3 defined `limit`, run 4 was its rerun.

prompt: Run from the top in a fresh kernel, Ana's notebook stops with `NameError: name 'limit' is not defined`. What is the cleanest fix?
hint: Settings belong where the notebook starts.

choices.text: Run the third cell first every time
choices.why: That is a ritual nobody else knows about.

choices.text: Move `limit = 10` to the top, with the other settings
choices.why: Right. Then page order is run order.

choices.text: Wrap the second cell in `try`/`except NameError`
choices.why: That hides the error and leaves `wet` undefined.

choices.text: Save the notebook with outputs so the answer is kept
choices.why: The answer is kept already; the notebook still cannot produce it.

prompt: A colleague's notebook gives 63 on their screen and fails on yours with `NameError`. What does that tell you about their notebook?
hint: Your run is from the top; theirs was not.

choices.text: Your Python is older than theirs
choices.why: A version difference would give another error, or none.

choices.text: Your copy of the file was corrupted somewhere on the way to you
choices.why: A corrupted file would not open at all.

choices.text: Its answer came from a run order the page does not hold
choices.why: Right. The 63 is real and the notebook cannot reproduce it.

choices.text: The 63 is wrong
choices.why: It may well be right; it just cannot be reproduced from the page.

prompt: You delete a cell that set `short_limit = 900`. What happens to `short_limit`?
hint: Where does the variable live?

choices.text: It disappears with the cell
choices.why: Deleting text does not touch the kernel's memory.

choices.text: It stays in the kernel
choices.why: Right. That is hidden state.

choices.text: It becomes `None`
choices.why: Nothing reassigns it.

choices.text: JupyterLab asks whether to keep it
choices.why: JupyterLab does not know which names a cell made.

prompt: Which command lists every name the kernel holds?
hint: A magic, with one `%`.

choices.text: `%reset -f`
choices.why: That deletes them.

choices.text: `%%writefile`
choices.why: That writes the cell to a file.

choices.text: `%who`
choices.why: Right; `%whos` adds types and values.

choices.text: `print(In)`
choices.why: `In` holds the inputs, not the names they made.

prompt: After `%reset -f`, a cell calling `is_short` fails. Why does the error name `trips` instead?
hint: Which name does `sum(is_short(t) for t in trips)` evaluate first?

choices.text: `is_short` survived the reset because functions are kept
choices.why: Functions are names like any other and go with the reset.

choices.text: The generator reads `trips` before it calls anything
choices.why: Right. Every name is gone; that one is met first.

choices.text: `trips` is a reserved name
choices.why: It is an ordinary variable.

choices.text: The reset only removed data, not code
choices.why: It removed every name.

prompt: Which of these leave the page showing something the kernel no longer agrees with, without any error? Choose all that apply.
hint: An error would be the honest case.

choices.text: Redefining a function after cells above used the old one
choices.why: Yes: those outputs came from the old version.

choices.text: Running `trips = trips[:1000]` near the end, then rerunning cells higher up
choices.why: Yes: they now work on a thousand rows.

choices.text: Running a cell that uses a name nobody defined
choices.why: That raises `NameError`, which is the honest case.

choices.text: Deleting the cell that defined a variable still in use
choices.why: Yes: the variable lives on with no source.

prompt: You change `bikes.py` and run `import bikes` again. `bikes.label(20)` still gives the old answer. Why?
hint: How many times does Python import a module in one process?

choices.text: The file was never saved to disk, only edited in the cell
choices.why: `%%writefile` printed `Overwriting bikes.py`.

choices.text: `import` reads a compiled copy from the previous day
choices.why: The module was loaded minutes ago, in this kernel.

choices.text: A module already loaded is not read again by `import`
choices.why: Right. `importlib.reload` or a restart reads it again.

choices.text: The function name is cached by JupyterLab
choices.why: JupyterLab caches nothing of the kernel's.

prompt: The cell magic that saves the rest of the cell to a file, instead of running it, is `%%___`.
hint: Write, and file.

prompt: A notebook reads `trips.csv`, cleans it and writes the result back to `trips.csv`. What goes wrong?
hint: Run it twice.

choices.text: The second run reads the first run's output, so the answers change
choices.why: Right. Never overwrite your input.

choices.text: pandas refuses to write over a file that it has just read
choices.why: Nothing refuses; that is the danger.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as the kernel is restarted between runs
choices.why: The file is outside the kernel; a restart reads the changed one.

choices.text: The file becomes JSON
choices.why: It stays whatever format the code writes.

prompt: What does Restart Kernel and Run All Cells… prove about a notebook when it finishes without an error?
hint: It replays the page.

choices.text: That its results will be the same on any computer
choices.why: Libraries, files and seeds can still differ elsewhere.

choices.text: That the page, run in order, produces its outputs
choices.why: Right: self-consistent, which is necessary and not the same as reproducible.

choices.text: That every result is correct
choices.why: A wrong calculation runs without errors too.

choices.text: That no cell was ever run out of order
choices.why: It cannot know the past; it makes the order irrelevant.

prompt: Which command runs a notebook top to bottom in a fresh kernel and writes the outputs back into the file?
hint: One of these does not save.

choices.text: `jupyter execute fixed.ipynb`
choices.why: It runs it and saves nothing.

choices.text: `jupyter nbconvert --clear-output --inplace fixed.ipynb`
choices.why: That empties the outputs without running anything.

choices.text: `jupyter nbconvert --to notebook --execute --inplace fixed.ipynb`
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `jupyter nbconvert --to notebook --execute --stdout fixed.ipynb > /dev/null`
choices.why: That runs it and throws the result away.

prompt: A notebook draws random numbers with no seed and passes Restart and Run All twice. Is it reproducible?
hint: Compare the two runs' numbers.

choices.text: Yes, because it ran without errors twice
choices.why: Running is not repeating the same numbers.

choices.text: Yes, if the kernel is the same
choices.why: A fresh kernel draws fresh numbers.

choices.text: No: it is self-consistent, but each run gives new numbers
choices.why: Right. Lesson 8 adds the seed.

choices.text: No, because random numbers make Run All fail
choices.why: They do not make anything fail.

prompt: Ana reruns a cell twice, changes no code, and saves. What does `git diff` show?
hint: What changes on every run?

choices.text: Nothing, since the code is the same
choices.why: git compares the JSON, outputs and counts included.

choices.text: Changed execution counts
choices.why: Right: `3` became `5`, twice.

choices.text: A new cell id for every cell
choices.why: Ids are kept once made.

choices.text: The whole file, because JSON is binary
choices.why: JSON is text; the diff is two lines.

prompt: What is the cost of committing notebooks with cleared outputs?
hint: What does somebody see when they open one from the repository?

choices.text: The notebook can no longer be run
choices.why: Clearing outputs leaves the code intact.

choices.text: git refuses files without outputs
choices.why: git stores any file.

choices.text: The cell ids are lost
choices.why: Ids stay; counts become `null`.

choices.text: Readers see no results until they run it
choices.why: Right, which is what they should do anyway.

prompt: Why does the `.gitignore` in `pydata` list `.venv/`?
hint: What is in it, and can it be rebuilt?

choices.text: It is hundreds of megabytes that a few commands rebuild
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: git cannot store files inside hidden directories
choices.why: It can; `.gitignore` itself is hidden.

choices.text: The environment holds the notebook outputs
choices.why: Outputs are inside the `.ipynb`.

choices.text: It contains passwords
choices.why: It contains libraries.

prompt: Put Ana's out-of-order session in the order it happened.
hint: The failed run took a count too.
items: Run the `wet` cell again and see 63
trap: Adding the limit cell before the failure is the tidy version of history, not the one the counts record.
